To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the change of monetary regime would have been very beneficial to households in the UK, that the volatility of consumption growth is higher in the more stable regime in the baseline calibration and that the observed reduction in consumption volatility is not necessarily a result of the change in the regime and could be due to other factors.
the welfare gains to households of the change in regime would be considerable, but that aggregate consumption volatility would actually be higher.

the welfare gains from the change in regime would have been substantial, but that the volatility of consumption growth in the aggregate could be higher in this more stable regime than it would have been in the 1980s regime.
In summary, our research is concerned with
understanding the interaction between microeconomic decisions and the macroeconomic regime.
the interaction between the macroeconomic environment and microeconomic behaviour in a setting where the microeconomic environment is changing in a significant way.
the implications of the interaction of microeconomic decisions facing individuals with the macroeconomic environment.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

there is little evidence of a direct link between the change in the regime for setting monetary policy, the fall in macroeconomic volatility and the increase in mortgage debt in the 1980s and 1990s, and therefore the welfare gains of this change are difficult to assess.
the fall in consumption volatility is a consequence of both lower macroeconomic volatility and the role of real world mortgages.
the observed decline in aggregate volatility cannot necessarily be explained as a consequence of the new monetary regime and the role of mortgages.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the new monetary policy framework has been a great benefit to households, but the macroeconomic consequences are more complex.
the new monetary regime has been beneficial for households, but it is not clear that it has been beneficial for the economy as a whole.
the welfare benefits of the new monetary policy regime have been large and have come at a cost of greater aggregate consumption volatility.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the microeconometric analysis of the role of mortgage contracts and the macroeconomic implications of the new regime need to consider the role of debt and the interaction between microeconomic behaviour and macroeconomic shocks.
the macroeconomic implications of mortgage contracts depend crucially on the nature of the macroeconomic environment.

the interaction of the macroeconomic environment and household decisions can be complex, and that the effects of changes in the macroeconomic environment may not be as straightforward as might be expected.
